passage:
Disha: dinner was a disaster 😔
Mehak: what happened??
Disha: Rajesh Uncle said young people don't know how things were, and went on about the leader. I said the numbers say otherwise. Voices got loud
Mehak: oof. did you win?
Disha: no. then I saw his hands shaking a bit. He said he lost his job in the nineties, so he's scared it'll happen again
Mehak: so that's what's under it
Disha: yeah. I said "I'll get more water, Uncle" and left the table before it got heated. Later I told him I heard him
Mehak: proud of you 🙂
Disha: I'd rather have peace at family dinners than a win 🙂

qa.q: What did Rajesh Uncle say he lost in the nineties?
qa.a: Rajesh Uncle said he lost his job in the nineties.

qa.q: What was Rajesh Uncle worried about, and how did Disha find out?
qa.a: He was afraid that losing his job would happen again; Disha saw his hands shaking and heard him say so.

qa.q: What did Disha do when the voices got loud, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Disha left the table with an excuse to get water before it heated up, keeping the relationship safe, which matters more than winning. 🙂

qa.q: How might Rajesh Uncle have felt about the numbers Disha quoted?
qa.a: Possibly as a young person dismissing what he lived through, which may be why his voice rose.

grounding: Disha clashes with an uncle over politics at dinner, listens for his worry, keeps facts calm and leaves respectfully.

passage: The last train was twenty minutes away, the platform was flooded, and Rafiq and Vinita had one umbrella between them. "How can you back that party?" Rafiq said, louder than intended. Vinita stiffened. Then Rafiq stopped and asked, "What matters most to you about it?" Vinita's voice softened. "Jobs. My father's factory is barely staying open." Rafiq nodded. "For me it's schools. My sisters' school has no science lab." They looked at the rain for a while. "So we both want people to be okay," Vinita said. "Deal: no converting each other," Rafiq said. "Deal." The train's light appeared, and they still had the fair to plan.

qa.q: How long until the last train?
qa.a: The last train was twenty minutes away.

qa.q: What did Rafiq feel when the argument began, and how did it change?
qa.a: Rafiq was heated and spoke too loudly, then became curious and asked what mattered most to Vinita.

qa.q: What agreement did they make, and why does it protect the friendship?
qa.a: They agreed not to convert each other, so the disagreement stays about views, while they share the values, wanting people to be okay. 😊

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt when Rafiq asked what mattered most to her?
qa.a: Relieved and listened to; Vinita's voice softened and she spoke about her father's factory.

grounding: A close friend backs the opposite party; Rafiq asks about the values behind the view and they agree not to convert each other.

passage: Rekha's thumb hovered over the share button. The video showed a crowd and a red caption: "THEY are coming for us. Share before it gets deleted!" Her chest was hot, and she wanted the whole class group to see it. Then she noticed the account had posted eleven angry videos that day, each ending with a link to buy a "support badge". Her cousin Charu was on the sofa. "Didi, look at this." Charu read the caption. "Where was it filmed?" "It doesn't say." "Then how do we know it's true? Whoever made this wants us furious." Rekha lowered the phone, searched for the clip, and found a news site saying it was from another city, years ago. She didn't share it.

qa.q: How many angry videos had the account posted that day?
qa.a: The account had posted eleven angry videos that day.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as her thumb hovered over share?
qa.a: Rekha felt angry, with a hot chest, and wanted the whole class group to see the clip.

qa.q: What could Rekha do before sharing anything similar?
qa.a: Pause, ask where and when it was filmed, and check a news source before passing it on.

qa.q: Why might the account owner want Rekha to be furious?
qa.a: The account posted many angry videos with a link to buy a badge, which suggests anger brings attention and money.

grounding: Memes and videos push Rekha to hate a group and share outrage; a pause and a check show it was made to anger and was old.

passage:
Teacher's note. In debate club today the class asked Keerthana, "Which side are you on?" It was said like a dare. Keerthana glanced at the floor, then said, "I agree with parts of both. I'm still learning." A few classmates rolled their eyes. Keerthana looked uneasy but did not pick a side. After class I said that "still learning" is an honest and respectable answer, and I gave Keerthana a short reading list with writers from several views. I also told the group that nobody has to join a team today. I'll ask next week what Keerthana found.
- Sahil, civics teacher

qa.q: What did Keerthana say when asked which side to join?
qa.a: Keerthana said, "I agree with parts of both. I'm still learning."

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling in that moment, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Keerthana felt pressured and uneasy, glancing at the floor, but held to the honest answer.

qa.q: What did Sahil do to help, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Sahil called "still learning" respectable and gave a reading list from several views, since reading widely is stronger than joining a team early.

qa.q: How might the classmates who asked see Keerthana's answer?
qa.a: Some may see it as dodging, as the eye-rolling suggests, though they may also just want company on their side.

grounding: Keerthana holds views that fit neither side and feels pressure to pick; the teacher affirms 'still learning' and offers wide reading.

passage: Trisha had spent two evenings reading the ward's water reports for her science project, and the numbers about the river made her want to do something. Deepika, from the next lane, told her about a peaceful cleanup walk on Sunday, with permission from the ward office. But there was a maths test on Monday and only two hours to spare. Trisha checked the notice, saw the organisers had marshals and drinking water, and showed it to Papa. "I'll be by the river bridge with Deepika, from ten till noon. I'll share my location." Papa read the notice twice. "Home by twelve-thirty." Trisha nodded, pulled on her old shoes, and put the revision notes in her bag.

qa.q: Who told Trisha about the cleanup walk?
qa.a: Deepika told Trisha about it.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling about the cause, and what showed it?
qa.a: Trisha felt moved and eager to act; two evenings of reading the water reports and the wish to do something show it.

qa.q: Which steps made Trisha's plan safe?
qa.a: Checking the notice for permission, marshals and water, telling Papa where and when, and sharing the location. 🙂

qa.q: How might Papa feel about being told the plan?
qa.a: Probably reassured and trusting, since Papa read the notice twice and agreed to a return time.

grounding: Trisha feels the pull of an environmental cause, learns the facts, picks a peaceful permitted walk and tells Papa where she will be.

passage: In the Lisbon school courtyard, Bao waved a phone. "Everyone's going to the rally on Saturday. Share this post so people know you're with us." Ines read the fierce words twice. Some of the phrases Ines did not understand at all. A tug of belonging pulled hard; all the friends had already shared it. "What does it say exactly?" Ines asked. "Just share, it's obvious." Ines frowned. "If it's obvious, you can explain it." Bao's face tightened. Ines put the phone down. "I'll come to hear what the rally is about. But I won't share until I understand it." Bao turned away, then muttered, "Fine."

qa.q: When was the rally?
qa.a: The rally was on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Ines feeling about the pressure, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ines felt torn between belonging and not understanding; the hard tug of belonging and the request to explain what the words meant show it.

qa.q: What could Ines do before deciding about sharing?
qa.a: Read the post carefully, ask questions, look for other sources or talk to a trusted adult, and only then decide.

qa.q: How might Bao feel about Ines's answer?
qa.a: Bao may feel hurt or worried about Ines drifting away, as the tightened face suggests; the muttered "Fine" shows some acceptance.

grounding: Friends push Ines to share something fierce and join a rally; Ines chooses to understand first and refuses to share.

passage: Sharmila, you said you might join the student march next month, so let me tell you about mine. I'm Mahima. At sixteen, I joined a march for a cause I cared about. The organiser put us school kids in the front row "for the cameras". There was no water, no marshals, and no plan for what to do if things got rough. When the crowd surged, my knees went weak. I remembered that I could leave. I took two friends by the arm and slipped down a side street. The organiser never looked for us. Later I learned that people who lead well look after the young ones first.

qa.q: Where did the organiser put the school students?
qa.a: The organiser put the school students in the front row.

qa.q: What did Mahima feel when the crowd surged, and what did Mahima remember?
qa.a: Mahima felt frightened, with weak knees, and remembered that Mahima could leave.

qa.q: What could Sharmila look for in a real leader before joining a march?
qa.a: A plan for safety, water, marshals and an exit, and signs that the leaders protect the young.

qa.q: How did the organiser seem to see the students?
qa.a: As a crowd for the cameras rather than people to look after, since they were placed in front with no safety and nobody searched for them.

grounding: Mahima recalls an organiser using students as a front-row crowd with no safety, and leaving when it felt unsafe.

passage:
Monday. Wasim showed the poster for a student walkout. "Just come. Everyone's going." Suraj's stomach dropped. What if the school punished them, or the police came? "I want to. I'm scared," Suraj said. Wasim shrugged, impatient.
Wednesday. Suraj stayed after class and asked the teacher what the school rules said about peaceful gatherings, and what students could do with permission. The teacher listed options and said the fear was worth listening to, not hiding.
Friday. Suraj signed the petition and joined the lunch-hour assembly the principal had allowed. Wasim stood beside Suraj, quieter than on Monday. "I'm glad you asked first," Wasim said.

qa.q: What did Suraj ask the teacher on Wednesday?
qa.a: Suraj asked what the school rules said about peaceful gatherings and what students could do with permission.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling on Monday, and why is fear not cowardice?
qa.a: Suraj was afraid of school punishment and police; the fear was honest information, and it led Suraj to check the rules.

qa.q: What choice did Suraj make in the end, and why did it fit?
qa.a: Suraj signed the petition and joined the allowed lunch-hour assembly, keeping to peaceful means with the fear taken seriously.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt on Monday compared with Friday?
qa.a: On Monday Wasim was impatient with Suraj's fear; by Friday Wasim was quieter and said "I'm glad you asked first".

grounding: Suraj fears school punishment and police action, uses the fear as information, learns the rules and joins peacefully.

passage:
Teacher's note. Elizabeth stayed back to tell me her parents had forbidden her to attend Saturday's protest. I saw disappointment first, then she said, "They are scared for me. I understand." She asked how she could still help. We talked about writing a piece for the school magazine about why the cause matters, and running a small fundraiser. Elizabeth said she would ask her parents to read the plan and to tell her what worried them most. I offered to help with the fundraiser table. I will check with her next week about how the talk went.
- Anjali, class teacher

qa.q: What safer ways to help did Elizabeth and the teacher discuss?
qa.a: They discussed writing a piece for the school magazine and running a small fundraiser.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling about her parents' ban, and what did she understand?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt disappointed but understood her parents were scared for her; she said "They are scared for me. I understand."

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do next if her parents still say no?
qa.a: Keep listening, keep offering safer ways to contribute, and show she takes the risks seriously. ❤️

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's parents feel when she brings the plan?
qa.a: Possibly relieved that she listens and wants to help safely, though the note does not show their reaction.

grounding: Parents forbid Elizabeth from a protest out of fear; Elizabeth hears them and proposes safer ways like writing and fundraising.

passage:
Teacher's note. Joseph, who leads the student group for the river cause, nodded off twice in my class this week, and his last test was well below his usual. When I asked, Joseph said, "I feel guilty when I stop. How can I rest while things are still bad?" I said a cause is carried by people who can keep going for years, and that studies and sleep are part of staying committed. Joseph looked unconvinced but agreed to hand two tasks to other members and take Saturday off. I'll ask on Monday how the weekend went. Joseph looked lighter leaving my room.
- Reena, class teacher

qa.q: What did Joseph say about resting?
qa.a: Joseph said, "I feel guilty when I stop. How can I rest while things are still bad?"

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling about rest, and what shows it?
qa.a: Joseph felt guilty about resting; the question about resting while things are bad, and the nodding off in class, show the strain.

qa.q: What did Reena suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Reena suggested handing two tasks to others and taking Saturday off, since a cause is carried by people who keep going for years, and studies and sleep are part of staying committed. 🤍

qa.q: How does Reena see Joseph's commitment?
qa.a: As valuable and worth protecting; Reena wants Joseph to last and checks on the weekend afterwards.

grounding: Joseph pours everything into a cause and feels guilty about resting; a teacher frames rest and studies as part of long-term commitment.
